name: Passive Voice
summary: Forming the passive correctly, especially for processes and reports.

paragraphs: Most sentences tell us who does something: The government built a new bridge. Sometimes, though, the person doing the action is unknown, unimportant or obvious, and what matters is the action itself or the thing affected. In these cases, English uses the passive voice: A new bridge was built.

The passive is especially useful in academic writing, and it is essential for describing processes and maps in Task 1. The good news is that every passive follows one simple formula. Once you know it, most passive errors become easy to spot.

blocks.title: The rule in one line
blocks.text: Passive = a form of be + past participle (is made, was built, should be reduced).

paragraphs: Examiners expect to see the passive in Task 1 process diagrams and maps, where what happens matters more than who does it. Using it correctly shows grammatical range. Using it incorrectly, for example by leaving out be, is one of the most common errors in IELTS writing.
In Task 2, the passive helps you sound more objective: It is often argued that… or Stricter laws should be introduced. These structures are natural in academic English.
In an active sentence, the subject does the action. In a passive sentence, the subject receives the action: the object of the active sentence moves to the front and becomes the new subject.
Compare the pairs below. The meaning is the same, but the focus changes from the doer to the action.

rows: The council built a new park.

paragraphs: The passive always has two parts: a form of be and a past participle. The most common mistake is to drop be and write only the main verb, especially after modal verbs such as should, must and can.
Without be, the sentence becomes active, and it suddenly means the subject is doing the action. Laws should introduce suggests the laws themselves will introduce something, which makes no sense.

items.text: First, the bottles collect from homes.
First, the bottles are collected from homes.

sections.title: Rule 2: Change be to change the tense
sections.label: Rule 2: Change be to change the tense

paragraphs: The past participle never changes in a passive sentence. The tense is shown entirely by be. So when you want a past passive, change is to was; for the present perfect, use has been or have been.
Remember that be must also agree with the subject: the bottle is washed, but the bottles are washed.

rows: Many trees have been cut down.
The factory had been demolished by 2020.
A new hospital will be built.
should / must / can be + past participle

sections.title: Rule 3: Use the past participle, not the base verb
sections.label: Rule 3: Use the past participle, not the base verb

paragraphs: The second part of the passive is the past participle. For regular verbs, this is the -ed form. For irregular verbs, you need to know the third form of the verb.
Mistakes such as is make or was build are common under time pressure. A quick check: the verb should sound natural after the word been (been made, been built).

items.text: The bricks are make from clay.
The bricks are made from clay.
The products are send to shops.
The products are sent to shops.

sections.title: Rule 4: Some verbs can never be passive
sections.label: Rule 4: Some verbs can never be passive

paragraphs: Only verbs that take an object can become passive. Verbs that describe something simply happening, such as happen, occur, rise, fall, arrive, die and disappear, have no object, so they have no passive form.
This trap is common in Task 1, because rise and fall can feel like something is being done to the numbers. It is not: the numbers rise and fall by themselves.

rows: The course is consisted of six units.
The course consists of six units.

sections.title: Rule 5: Mention the doer only when it matters
sections.label: Rule 5: Mention the doer only when it matters

paragraphs: In a passive sentence, you can say who did the action with by: The bridge was designed by a Japanese company. Most of the time, though, the doer is left out because it is obvious, unknown or unimportant.
Include by + doer only when it adds useful information. In process descriptions it is usually unnecessary: The bottles are collected by workers adds nothing important.

items.text: The painting was stolen in 1990. (doer unknown)
The new airport was designed by a Japanese company. (useful detail)
The leaves are dried in the sun. (by workers is not needed)

sections.title: Rule 6: The passive in process diagrams
sections.label: Rule 6: The passive in process diagrams

paragraphs: Process diagrams show how something is made or how a system works. Because the focus is on the stages, not the people, the passive is the natural choice, usually in the present simple.
Combine it with sequence words to guide the reader smoothly through the stages.

rows: First, To begin with, In the first stage
Next, Then, After that, Following this

items.text: First, the tea leaves are picked by hand.
Next, they are spread out and dried.
Finally, the dried leaves are packed and sold.

sections.title: Rule 7: The passive in map descriptions
sections.label: Rule 7: The passive in map descriptions

paragraphs: Map questions in Task 1 show how a place has changed over time. Again, the focus is on what was done, not who did it, so the passive is used: was built, was demolished, was replaced, was converted, was expanded.
Use the past simple passive for changes between two past dates, and the past perfect passive with by + a past year.

rows: The warehouse was converted into apartments.
Something took the place of another
The trees were replaced by a road.

sections.title: Rule 8: “It is said that…” in Task 2
sections.label: Rule 8: “It is said that…” in Task 2

paragraphs: Academic writers often present common opinions with an impersonal passive: It is argued that…, It is believed that…, It is often said that…. This sounds more objective than People say….
The pattern is fixed: It + is + past participle + that. Do not leave out is.

items.text: It is widely believed that technology improves education.
It believed that exams cause stress.
It is believed that exams cause stress.
It has been argued that cities should ban cars.

blocks.title: Is located
blocks.text: To describe where something is, use is located or is situated. Locate on its own means “to find”, so The factory locates near the river is wrong. Write: The factory is located near the river.

paragraphs: Here is how the passive appears in real IELTS writing. Notice how often the doer is left out.

rows: The leaves are dried and then rolled.
A new road was built to the north of the village.
By 2020, the factory had been demolished.
By + past year: past perfect passive
It is often argued that university should be free.

paragraphs: These five errors are among the most common passive mistakes in IELTS essays.

rows: The water is pump into a tank.
The water is pumped into a tank.
The accident was happened at night.
The school locates near the river.
The school is located near the river.

paragraphs: Use this routine whenever the subject of a sentence is not the one doing the action.

steps: Find sentences where something is being made, built, collected or introduced.
Check both parts: a form of be + a past participle.
Check that the verb can be passive at all. Rise, fall, happen and occur cannot.

furtherStudy.title: Purdue OWL: Active Versus Passive Voice
furtherStudy.description: When to choose the passive in academic writing.

furtherStudy.title: Purdue OWL: Passive Verbs
furtherStudy.description: How the passive is formed in each tense.

cards.why: Paper does not make anything; it is made by someone. This needs be + past participle.
The tower did not complete itself; it was completed by builders. In 1889 also calls for the past form was.

cards.front: Stricter laws should ____ to protect forests.
cards.why: Laws do not introduce anything themselves. After should, the passive is be + past participle.
Happen has no object, so it can never be passive.
Schools are built by someone, so we need the passive. Since 2010 calls for the present perfect: have been built.

cards.front: After that, the fruit ____ into small pieces.
cards.why: Cut is irregular: cut → cut → cut. There is no word cutted.

cards.front: Unemployment ____ sharply after the factory closed.
cards.why: Rise has no object, so it cannot be passive. Numbers rise by themselves.

cards.front: It ____ widely believed that exercise improves mood.
cards.why: The impersonal passive pattern is It + is + past participle + that.

cards.front: The museum ____ in the center of the old town.
cards.why: To describe position, we use is located. Locate alone means “to find”.

cards.front: In the next stage, the bottles ____ with clean water.
cards.why: The passive needs the past participle (washed), not the base verb (wash).
